query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as-deposited, non-equiatomic Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si high-entropy alloys that exhibit a first-order magnetostructural transition, the governing factor for low-applied-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis is the nanoscale density and coherence of interphase boundaries between an ordered hexagonal magnetocaloric phase and a coexisting disordered matrix (or competing phase). Increasing the density of imperfectly coherent interphase boundaries at fixed global composition lowers the nucleation barrier for the transition and distributes transformation pathways, thereby reducing hysteresis and broadening the entropy-change profile under low fields while enabling more reversible cycling.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si alloy film/foil with mixed short-range order, finite defect density, and partial coexistence of an ordered hexagonal magnetocaloric phase with a disordered matrix; mechanically stable and free of rare-earth elements.
generation.intervention: At fixed average composition, tune the as-deposited microstructure by varying substrate bias energy during magnetron sputtering (low-bias to increase fine grain size, defect density, and interphase boundary density; high-bias to promote larger grains and higher coherence/ordering), without changing thickness or composition. Optionally confirm with a brief low-temperature anneal that does not induce long-range coarsening.
generation.conditions: Low applied magnetic fields typical of device operation (<1 T), cyclic magnetization–demagnetization near the transition temperature; ambient pressure; thin film/foil geometry to enable rapid heat exchange; measurements performed over multiple cycles to assess reversibility.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale interphase boundaries (including twin boundaries) between the ordered hexagonal magnetocaloric phase and the coexisting disordered/alternate phase; their density and coherence length, and the elastic/magnetic exchange mismatch across these boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Higher interphase boundary density provides abundant, elastically compliant and magnetically frustrated nucleation sites that lower the effective barrier and latent-heat bottleneck of the first-order magnetostructural transition. Reduced coherence across boundaries diminishes interfacial elastic energy and exchange-locking, distributing transformation over a wider temperature/field range. This yields smaller hysteresis and a broader, more reversible entropy-change profile under low fields, at the cost of a lower peak ΔS, but with increased usable refrigerant capacity in cyclic, low-field operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a high-bias (more ordered, larger-grain, lower-boundary-density) baseline, the low-bias (higher-boundary-density) sample will show: (i) reduced thermal and field hysteresis of the magnetostructural transition; (ii) a broader ΔS(T) peak under low fields, with improved reversibility over repeated cycles; (iii) a lower field threshold to achieve a given transformed fraction; and (iv) a trade-off of reduced peak ΔS but increased relative cooling power in low-field cycling due to the broadened response.
generation.baseline: As-deposited sample with lower interphase boundary density (larger grains, higher coherence) shows a sharper, larger ΔS peak tied to a first-order transition, but with larger hysteresis and higher field threshold, and poorer reversibility in cyclic low-field operation.
generation.boundary: Applies to non-equiatomic Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si compositions that exhibit a first-order magnetostructural transition with coexisting phases in the as-deposited state; thin geometries enabling rapid heat exchange; low-field operation (<1 T). Predictions may not hold if the material is fully amorphous (no ordered phase), fully single-phase and highly ordered (no coexistence), or if interphase boundary density becomes so high that long-range transformation is suppressed. Large residual stresses or chemical segregation that dominate magnetic exchange can also override the mediated effect.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative magnitudes (fractional hysteresis reduction, ΔS broadening, and relative cooling power gains) are uncertain without empirical calibration. The optimal boundary density for minimizing hysteresis while preserving sufficient ΔS is unknown, and residual stress or defect pinning introduced by deposition could produce competing effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-deposited Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si films/foils with identical average composition, thickness, and deposition temperature, but different substrate bias (low vs high) to produce higher vs lower interphase boundary densities. Quantify microstructure and then measure magnetocaloric response under low fields and cyclic operation. Keep all other variables constant.
measurements: TEM/HAADF-STEM to map interphase boundary density, twin boundary density, and coherence length distributions
XRD (including in-situ vs T) to identify phase fractions and transition signature; Scherrer/Williamson–Hall analysis for coherence length
Magnetization vs temperature (M–T) under various low fields, with cyclic hysteresis loops; determine thermal and field hysteresis widths
Isothermal magnetization curves for Maxwell-derived ΔS(T,H) under low fields
Direct differential scanning calorimetry (if feasible) to assess latent heat and its change with microstructure
Relative cooling power (RCP) and cycle-to-cycle reversibility under low-field cycling
Residual stress assessment (XRD sin²ψ or wafer curvature) to control for stress effects
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, at fixed composition, increasing interphase boundary density does not reduce hysteresis, does not broaden ΔS(T) under low fields, and does not lower the field threshold for partial transformation—while microstructural characterization confirms the intended change in boundary density—then the hypothesis is falsified. Alternatively, if similar changes are only observed when composition is modified but not when microstructure is tuned at fixed composition, the governing role of interphase boundaries is falsified.
